To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
We present a detailed analysis of the Raman spectra of mechanically exfoliated graphene ribbons with widths ranging from ~15 to 160 nm.

the D-line intensity in mechanically exfoliated graphene ribbons is strongly dependent on light polarization and that the edge disorder correlation length in these ribbons is approximately one order magnitude larger than in ribbons fabricated by etching techniques.

the Raman spectra of graphene nanoribons (GNR) with widths ranging from about 15 to 150 nm, which are fabricated by exfoliation of graphene flakes, exhibit a strong polarization dependence of the D-line, which is absent in GNR fabricated by etching.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of graphene nanoribbon-based field-effect transistors (FETs) as a novel type of nanoscale electronic devices.
the synthesis and characterization of graphene nanoribbon (GNR) based field effect transistors (FETs).

the development of a new type of graphene nanoribons (GNRs) with a high degree of structural perfection and a large aspect ratio, which are produced using a novel method based on mechanical exfoliation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
graphene ribbons are more ordered when they are fabricated without etching.
the graphene nanoribons presented here are of high quality, and that they are suitable for the study of edge physics and edge effects in nanoscale graphene devices.
the D-line intensity of the graphene nanoribons is strongly dependent on their width and the polarization direction of incident light.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have been able to show that graphene ribbons with a width of only 15 nm can be fabricated by mechanical exfoliation.
the Raman spectroscopy is a useful and powerful technique to study the properties of graphene ribbons.
Raman spectroscopy is a powerful tool to investigate graphene nano-ribbons and that we can use it to extract information about the edge disorder and the crystallographic orientation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the edge structure of non-etched ribbons is much more regular than that of etched ribbons.
we were able to fabricate graphene ribbons of a width down to 15 nm, where the D line is still not visible.
Raman scattering is a very useful tool for probing graphene nanoribons, and in particular, it is very sensitive to edge defects.
